I've been thinking for awhile about creating a VM in Virtualbox with which to test out some of the Gaming options for a Linux Distro. I don't see many choices when I search Distrowatch for 'Distribution Category'='Gaming', & that's usually my go-to place for Linux Distros to try. Years ago, I recall there being Gaming-specific Distros, but I guess that's no more. So this leads me to ask, how to best get started with quality Gaming with Linux? Thanks in advance of what I'm sure will be a flood of replies- hehe. :-)
What's the best way to get started with Linux Gaming in a VM?

Steam has a native Linux client, and its Windows client works well in WINE. Check WineDB to see if whatever Windows games you want work well in WINE or how to set them up in WINE.

As for running Steam in a VM, a quick search gave me this and this. I haven't actually looked at them (I'm leaving soon), but the Youtube video claims 95% native performance. You might need some extra hardware to do it though.
I haven't played with SteamOS yet but if I wanted a Linux gaming system I'd start with that.
SteamOS is for building a console for the TV. I run it on my HTPC and would not recommend it for desktops.

Yeah, there are no gaming-specific distros any more, or at least, none in the main stream. Though I suppose, actually, SteamOS would qualify as a gaming-specific distro, but it's also very Steam specific obviously.

If I were going to try what you're talking about, I'd just stick with one of the "big" names. Arch, Ubuntu, Mint, etc. Maybe Elementary as well. There's a method of creating a pass-through in the VM so that it gets better access to the hardware, but I'm not familiar enough with the specifics to explain how. Even with the pass-through, you'll probably lose a bit of performance by running in a VM - but the it will probably vary game-to-game.

I'm not advocating it and it may not be the case anymore, but the last time I gave a swing at gaming in a linux-host-windows-client vm I had a better experience with vmware workstation as opposed to virtualbox. It makes sense that the for-profit guys offer the snazzier hypervisor, but again, this is anecdotal and based on tinkering circa 2010. These days I don't even bother. If It's not native and I can't get it going under wine and I reeeaaally want to play it i keep a dedicated win7 box for that.
